title: PWHL adds Kilmer Sports Ventures, Ilitch Companies as first outside investors
content:
Just one month after completing its third season, the Professional Women’s Hockey League has added its first outside investment, the league announced Monday morning.

Kilmer Sports Ventures, which is led by Toronto businessman Larry Tanenbaum, and Ilitch Companies, the parent company of the NHL’s Detroit Red Wings and MLB’s Detroit Tigers, have joined the league as partners.

According to Sportico, the league has received a $100 million investment; however, financial terms were not disclosed in the league’s announcement. This is the first time the PWHL, which was established in 2023, has accepted outside capital.

“It’s hard to overstate the significance of this,” Stan Kasten, a member of the PWHL’s advisory board who is also the president of MLB’s Los Angeles Dodgers, told The Athletic. “It really says more than any press release could about how far we’ve come and what the future holds when we have people of this stature stepping up and telling the world of what they have seen and what they believe our future is.”

According to Kasten, the league opened up a round of investment and ended with two “big-time, savvy, world-class” investors. The money isn’t earmarked for anything specific, Kasten said, but will “help us continue the momentum.”

“We got more than what we needed to continue our growth,” he said, “and that’s all to the benefit of the whole league.”

Kilmer Sports owns a stake in Maple Leaf Sports and Entertainment, the parent company of the NHL’s Toronto Maple Leafs and the NBA’s Toronto Raptors. Kilmer Sports also recently paid a $50 million expansion fee to bring the WNBA to Toronto with the Toronto Tempo. Ilitch Companies is based in Detroit and run by Chris Ilitch, who also manages Little Caesars Arena, home of the Red Wings and the PWHL’s new expansion franchise in Detroit, as well as other entertainment venues across the region.

“Building world-class women’s sports organizations that inspire the next generation of athletes, fans, and leaders is how you create something that truly lasts. We saw that opportunity first with the Tempo, Canada’s first WNBA team, and now we’re proud to deepen that commitment through this significant investment in the PWHL,” Tanenbaum said in a release. “What Mark Walter and PWHL senior leadership have built so quickly is incredible, and we’re honored to be part of this league and everything it stands for.”

Since its inception, the league has operated under a single-entity ownership model, meaning Walter — the billionaire owner of the Dodgers — and his wife, Kimbra, own the league and its franchises. There has been no change to the league’s operations, with Amy Scheer (executive vice president of business operations) and Jayna Hefford (executive vice president of hockey operations) reporting to the advisory board, which includes Kasten, tennis legend Billie Jean King and King’s partner, Ilana Kloss.

Kasten told The Athletic there are no current plans to solicit individual franchise owners, which is a departure from the traditional ownership model used by major North American sports leagues.

“This is more about being able to tap Larry and Chris’s networks, being able to get advice from their experience,” Kasten said. “(They are) deeply embedded in hockey and in women’s sports. … Having one American investor like this and one Canadian investor like this, we thought, was the perfect combination for us at this time to continue our growth, and we couldn’t be more excited.”

The PWHL officially dropped the puck in January 2024 with six original franchises and expanded for the first time ahead of the 2025-26 season, adding teams in Vancouver and Seattle.

The league has since experienced record growth in its third season, surpassing one million fans in attendance in a season for the first time. Average attendance rose 28 percent from 7,230 spectators in 2024-25 to 9,304 this season — a 71 percent increase over the inaugural season in 2024.

Next season, the league will officially welcome teams in Detroit; Hamilton, Ontario; Las Vegas and San Jose, increasing its size to 12 teams spread more widely across North America. Initially, Kasten said he thought it would take 10 or 12 years to reach that size.

“But it’s all just happening,” he said. “The interest is there, the support is there from various marketplaces, and so this was a good time to bring in this additional support and let us continue on our path.”
